title: Syntax that says a lot
description: References, pointers, const, auto, range-based for loops, lambdas and namespaces.

content.title: References and pointers
content.body:
Two symbols change everything in C++:
- int& r = x; declares a reference: r is another name for x. Changing r changes x.
- int* p = &x; declares a pointer: p holds the address of x. *p is the value at that address, and changing *p changes x. A pointer can also point to nothing: nullptr.

Careful: & and * mean different things in a declaration (int& r, int* p) and in an expression (&x is "the address of x", *p is "the value pointed to by p").

By default, function parameters are copies. A parameter declared with & works on the caller's variable instead.

content.explanation: r is a reference: another name for x. Assigning to r assigns to x.
p holds the address of x, and *p is the variable at that address: x itself. So *p = 7 changes x.
n is a copy of a, so a does not change. With void addOne(int& n), the function would change a, and a would be 2.

content.question: Why do C++ functions often take parameters like const std::string& name?

choices.text: To avoid copying the string, while promising not to change it
Because strings cannot be passed any other way
To make the string modifiable by the function

content.explanation: & avoids a copy, which can be costly for a long string, and const guarantees the caller's string is not modified. It is the usual way to pass big objects that are only read.

content.title: Modern C++
content.body:
Since C++11, the language has many features that make code shorter and safer:
- auto: the compiler deduces the type, as in auto count = 3;
- Range-based for: for (auto item : items) goes through a container.
- Lambdas: [capture](parameters) { body } is a small function written inline; the capture list says which variables it takes from around it.
- nullptr: the null pointer, safer than the old NULL or 0.

The standard library lives in the std namespace: std::string, std::vector, std::cout...

content.explanation: auto n makes n a copy of each element, so the vector is unchanged. for (auto& n : v) would give a reference to each element, and v would become 2, 4, 6.
[factor] captures a copy of factor when the lambda is created, when it is still 3. With [&factor], the lambda would see the new value and print 20.

content.question: What do std and :: mean in std::cout?

choices.text: cout is in the std namespace (the standard library); :: reaches a name inside a scope
std is a class and cout one of its methods
std means "standard output", and :: calls it
It is a pointer to cout

content.explanation: :: is the scope resolution operator. Namespaces avoid name clashes: your own cout would not conflict with std::cout.
